entry.title: Building natural wealth
entry.content:
Home / Opinion / Editorial / Building natural wealthBuilding natural wealth

Environmental accounts can inform policy decisions

premium

India's new environmental accounting strategy aims to measure the economic value of natural resources and ecosystem services to support sustainable development and better policy decisions.

Business Standard Editorial Comment3 min read Last Updated : Oct 18 2026 | 10:46 PM ISTThe Ministry of Statistics and Programme Implementation’s (Mospi’s) new “Strategy for Environmental Economic Accounts in India 2026-30” is an attempt to measure the country’s natural resources and ecosystem services in a more systematic accounting framework. The rationale is straightforward. Natural resources form the backbone of economic activities, but their depletion and the services provided by ecosystems are not adequately reflected in conventional measures such as gross domestic product (GDP). The timing is important. As India pursues faster growth amid increasing pressure on land and water, policymakers need to know not only how much the economy produces, but also what it is consuming from its natural-resource base. The strategy follows the United Nations System of Environmental-Economic Accounting (SEEA) and builds on Mospi’s work since 2018. The pollination account can illustrate why this matters. Mospi estimates the value of pollination services at ₹2.66 trillion in 2021-22, up from ₹1.15 trillion in 2012-13, equivalent to roughly 8-10 per cent of crop output. Conventional agricultural accounts capture the value of the crop, but not the ecosystem service that contributes to producing it. Making such a contribution visible can strengthen the economic case for protecting pollinators, supporting beekeeping and designing pollinator-friendly agricultural policies. The same logic applies to water accounts, which can help policymakers assess resource use and groundwater stress, and also to mineral accounts, which can track extraction, depletion and discoveries.  The strategy also has a wider development role. Mospi estimates that environmental accounts can support the assessment of about 40 global indicators across nine Sustainable Development Goals. The new road map expands the coverage to carbon stocks, biodiversity and environment-related economic activities, potentially making environmental information more useful for decisions extending well beyond the environment ministry. International experience shows what such accounting can achieve. The United Kingdom (UK) natural-capital accounts estimated the annual value of ecosystem services at £41 billion in 2023, while the asset value of natural capital was estimated at £1.6 trillion. Such estimates bring nature into discussions of national wealth rather than treating it only as an environmental concern.  But measurement is only the first hurdle. Implementation is the harder test. India has undertaken environmental-accounting studies at state level for years, but differences in concepts, definitions, and methods have prevented these efforts from being aggregated into a consistent national picture. Only 18 states and Union Territories have so far constituted inter-departmental groups on environmental accounting, while Mospi itself identifies a shortage of expertise in the SEEA framework. The next five years should, therefore, focus less on adding accounts for their own sake and more on making them comparable, timely and usable. Common definitions, interoperable state databases, spatially consistent data, and trained officials are necessary. Most importantly, the accounts must enter the decision-making process — from groundwater allocation and mining permits to land-use planning and forest restoration. The real success of the 2026-30 strategy will not be the number of accounts published but whether the depletion of natural wealth can be arrested for sustainable development.   Topics : BS Opinion Business Standard Editorial Comment Natural resources Sustainable Development Goals

entry.title: Waiving double standards
entry.content:
Home / Opinion / Editorial / Waiving double standardsWaiving double standards

Mr Trump discovers merits of national interest

premium

US President Donald Trump's decision to temporarily waive sanctions on Russian oil imports has raised questions over Washington's policy consistency and its commitment to Ukraine | Photo: White House

Business Standard Editorial Comment3 min read Last Updated : Oct 18 2026 | 10:45 PM ISTUnited States (US) President Donald Trump’s decision to waive sanctions on Russian imports under a congressional law must be seen as a relief for India both in terms of its oil-import policy and for concluding the long-awaited trade deal, which had stalled mainly on this account as well as Section 301 investigations. On a broader canvas, the 60-day waiver demonstrates the Trump regime’s double standards, ratchets up strategic uncertainty over US support for ally Ukraine in its war against Russia, and generally raises global misgivings about US reliability as an ally.  The Lindsey O Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act, 2026, gave the President the powers to impose 100 per cent tariffs on major Russian oil buyers such as India and China, to deprive Moscow of revenue to finance its war against Ukraine. When the war broke out in February 2022, and the West drew down Russian oil and gas purchases in solidarity with Ukraine, India chose to accept the deep discounts offered by a traditional ally. This move was excoriated by Mr Trump, who imposed an additional punitive 25 per cent tariff on Indian imports in August 2025, later lifted following an interim trade framework in February this year. India’s imports of Russian oil rose steadily from about 2 per cent of all its purchase of crude oil to almost 50 per cent, as New Delhi sought to parry sharply rising global oil prices as a result of Western sanctions. Despite the fulminations from the White House, the validity of this approach, driven by national interests, was underlined by the fact that the US continued to import uranium from Russia despite the war.  This latest waiver, driven by electoral considerations ahead of November mid-term polls and signed a day before the 30-day enforcement deadline, has undermined even further the logical tenability of US objections to India’s imports of Russian oil. The blockade of the Strait of Hormuz following US-Israel attacks on Iran has exerted upward pressure on prices of oil products, and like others, the American people are feeling the pinch. Diesel prices have risen 66-68 per cent over the year, driving up prices all round. The grounds for the waiver, enabled by Section 115 of the Lindsey Graham Act, were prepared on October 9, when the US Treasury issued a temporary licence allowing the sale and import of Russian diesel into the global market until April 7, 2027.  The agreement with Russia will immediately provide the US 300,000 tonnes of diesel, followed by 500,000 tonnes in November and one million tonnes subsequently. Russia will also release 3 million tonnes, depending on the state of its refineries (some of which were recently attacked by Ukraine).  This remarkable geostrategic pivot is also driven by Mr Trump’s tensions with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy, who has accused the US administration of scaling back military support and intelligence sharing. Delays in supplying promised Patriot missiles and deteriorating Starlink satellite services, which have impacted drone performance and battlefield communications, have been notable setbacks for Ukraine of late. As US allies add their voice to lawmakers, including some Republicans, on the amorality of the latest waiver, it is ironic that Mr Trump should offer the national-interest counter-argument — which he emphatically rejected in India’s case a year ago.   Topics : Donald Trump BS Opinion Business Standard Editorial Comment Russia US Russia Russia Ukraine Conflict

entry.title: Steel ambitions
entry.content:
Home / Opinion / Editorial / Steel ambitionsSteel ambitions

2047 goals must balance capacity expansion with clean tech

premium

Steelmaking inputs account for an estimated 65-70 per cent of costs, and India imports around 92 per cent of its coking coal requirements

Business Standard Editorial Comment3 min read Last Updated : Oct 15 2026 | 10:04 PM ISTThe draft “National Steel Policy: Vision 2047” sets out an ambitious road map for India’s steel industry. It targets an increase in crude steel capacity from about 220 million tonnes (mt) in 2025-26 to 604 mt by 2047, with production projected at 531 mt and finished steel demand at 505 mt. The scale of the proposed expansion reflects the sector’s importance to infrastructure and manufacturing. These projections assume annual gross domestic product (GDP) growth of around 7 per cent and capacity utilisation of 88 per cent. With construction and infrastructure accounting for roughly two-thirds of steel consumption, public investment will remain a key driver of demand. Notably, the policy recognises that technology and material substitution could alter future requirements. Its proposal to review the projections periodically, preferably every five years, must be welcomed.  However, raw-material security remains a challenge. Steelmaking inputs account for an estimated 65-70 per cent of costs, and India imports around 92 per cent of its coking coal requirements. The policy seeks to expand domestic mining, improve beneficiation, develop overseas mineral assets and strengthen supply arrangements. These are necessary steps, but the projected expansion also exposes a contradiction. Coking coal requirements are projected to rise from 72 mt to 236 mt by 2047, with the basic oxygen furnace route retaining a 55 per cent share of production. Unless the transition to less carbon-intensive technologies gathers pace, capacity expansion could deepen import dependence and increase emissions. The policy targets a reduction in emissions intensity from 2.54 tonnes of carbon dioxide per tonne of crude steel to 1.54 tonnes by 2047. It proposes greater use of scrap, renewable electricity, hydrogen-based direct reduced iron, and carbon capture, utilisation and storage. Falling renewable-power and storage costs may improve the economics of cleaner steelmaking. Project appraisals must, therefore, compare the full life-cycle costs of competing technologies rather than assume that conventional production will remain the cheapest option.  Trade policy must reinforce this transition towards competitiveness. The draft rightly calls for balancing protection against unfair imports with affordable inputs for downstream users. Safeguards may be justified where injury from unfair trade is established, but protection cannot become a substitute for productivity improvements. With the EU Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism linking market access to embedded emissions, producers must factor carbon costs and cleaner technology into decisions on new plants. More countries are likely to adopt similar measures. Export ambitions also depend on cost competitiveness. India’s steel exports fell from 10.78 mt in 2020-21 to 6.60 mt in 2025-26, while the policy envisages exports of 45 mt by 2047. Achieving that target will require reliable quality, efficient logistics and access to overseas markets.  Finally, support for specialty steel, research & development, digitalisation and cleaner technologies should be judged by results. In this regard, it is also worth debating whether steel needs the planned production-linked incentives. Success will come from commercially viable products, better productivity, and the use of modern technology. The real test, therefore, will be whether the industry can expand while lowering costs, reducing emissions, and moving up the value chain.     Topics : BS Opinion National Steel Policy Steel Industry Steel productions

entry.title: Exit strategy
entry.content:
Home / Opinion / Editorial / Exit strategyExit strategy

Govt must push its disinvestment agenda aggressively

premium

The strategic sale of IDBI Bank also underscores sustained foreign investor interest in India’s financial sector (Image: Bloomberg)

Business Standard Editorial Comment3 min read Last Updated : Oct 15 2026 | 9:57 PM ISTMarking a major step in the government’s privatisation and disinvestment programme, the Cabinet Committee on Economic Affairs chaired by Prime Minister Narendra Modi finally approved the strategic sale of IDBI Bank, after much back and forth, on Wednesday. Once completed, the transaction will be the largest foreign direct investment (FDI) in India’s financial sector to date. Under the arrangement, the Union government will sell a 30.48 per cent stake in the bank and Life Insurance Corporation a 30.24 per cent stake. They currently hold 45.48 per cent and 49.24 per cent, respectively. Toronto-based Fairfax Financial Holdings will acquire the combined 60.72 per cent for ₹52,878 crore, or about $5.6 billion.  The strategic sale of IDBI Bank also underscores sustained foreign investor interest in India’s financial sector. RBL Bank, Yes Bank and Shriram Finance have attracted substantial foreign investment in recent years. Fairfax itself has significant holdings in entities such as CSB Bank and IIFL Finance. As reported by this newspaper, Fairfax, which holds a 40 per cent stake in CSB Bank, has been given the option of either exiting the bank or merging it with IDBI Bank to meet regulatory requirements. It will eventually also have to reduce its stake in IDBI Bank to 26 per cent. A glide path for this reduction is likely to be worked out in consultation with the Reserve Bank of India (RBI). The RBI will need to closely monitor Fairfax’s holdings across these financial institutions.  The approval of the IDBI Bank deal is significant on several counts. The government’s record in strategic sales has not been very encouraging. Only 21 such transactions, including the IDBI Bank deal, have taken place in the past 26 years, partly reflecting limited activity during the United Progressive Alliance government’s tenure. Given the complexities involved in the strategic sale of a bank, it is hoped this will mark a new beginning. The government’s policy, as announced in the Union Budget for 2021-22, is that central public-sector enterprises (CPSEs) will have a bare minimum presence in strategic sectors. The rest will be privatised, merged with other CPSEs, or closed. In non-strategic sectors, CPSEs are to be privatised or closed. However, it is fair to argue that progress on this has so far been limited. Data compiled by the Sixteenth Finance Commission showed that the total number of CPSEs increased from 717 in 2020-21 to 748 in 2023-24. The government’s equity in CPSEs also increased substantially. Notably, over 200 CPSEs made losses during this period.  Government participation in commercial activity not only ties up resources but also often burdens the Budget. The government, for instance, infused about ₹25,000 crore into IDBI Bank between 2010 and 2020. The bank has since recovered from the bad-loan crisis and posted strong numbers last financial year. Its gross non-performing asset ratio declined to 2.3 per cent from over 30 per cent in September 2018. Once the deal is completed, the government must also aim to sell its residual 15 per cent stake in the bank. It should pursue more such deals and also sell equity in listed CPSEs to push the disinvestment programme. This will not only reduce its footprint in commercial activity, but also raise funds for physical and social infrastructure. Listed companies in which government holdings exceed 75 per cent, including public-sector banks such as Indian Overseas Bank and Uco Bank, should be early candidates for stake sales.     Topics : BS Opinion IDBI Bank privatisation Stake sale Life Insurance Corporation

entry.title: Mind the gap
entry.content:
Home / Opinion / Editorial / Mind the gapMind the gap

Travel survey underlines public-transport shortage

premium

Only 15% of Indian workers use public transport, while 43% rely on two-wheelers, highlighting gaps in urban mobility, according to an NSO survey. | Image: PTI

Business Standard Editorial Comment3 min read Last Updated : Oct 14 2026 | 10:19 PM ISTThe first all-India survey on household travel, conducted by the National Statistics Office between July 2025 and July 2026, offers useful pointers for transportation and urban planners. Covering over 14,000 villages and 10,000 urban blocks, the broad findings suggest that the average Indian commuter is disproportionately dependent on personal and private transport. In other words, public transport in India is woefully inadequate in serving the needs of a burgeoning working population.  Only 15 per cent of workers use public transport — buses, trains, or trams. Forty-three per cent use two-wheelers and 3 per cent cars. The rest either walk — especially in rural areas — or use bicycles or cycle rickshaws. Over 57 per cent of workers travel more than 1 km to their workplace. But average commute times are relatively short — 25 minutes, on average, with 27 minutes in urban areas and 23 minutes in rural areas. The low rate of women’s workforce participation is evident in a wide gender-mobility gap, with 62 per cent of male workers undertaking daily work trips as against 42 per cent of female workers. Overall, travelling to work is an expensive proposition for the average Indian. According to the survey, workers spend roughly ₹785 a month on fixed-workplace travel, with urban workers shelling out a steep ₹1,044, compared with ₹612 for rural workers. Thus, commuting accounts for a significant proportion of average monthly wages, which stand at around ₹22,000 for regular salaried employees and ₹15,000 for the self-employed.  The big picture explains the skewed and inequitable process of urbanisation, where affluent suburban agglomerations and factories located on the edge of large towns and cities tend to be surrounded by shanties and slums to house the supporting workforce. The average worker cannot afford to live too far away from her or his place of work. This unbalanced pattern of urban development, whether in India’s older cities or the newer ones, is socially suboptimal. Workers are forced to live in grossly unhealthy environments, with scant access to basic necessities, side by side with middle-class and wealthy Indians. The survey, therefore, underlines the need for integrated urban planning. The provision of a safe and well-distributed transport system that radiates from city centres to the outskirts, supplemented with genuine low-cost housing, would go a long way towards expanding the ambit of employment for both men and women — a model that Mumbai and Kolkata follow — though imperfectly — with their suburban train systems.  The inadequacy of public transport highlighted in the survey also plays its role in the chronic problem of pollution. For overnight travel, the survey shows that buses rather than the electrified Indian railway system are the preferred mode of transport. Workers travelling more than 1 km to the workplace rely disproportionately on fossil fuel-powered two-wheelers and cars. Electric-vehicle penetration is still below 10 per cent in both categories. The resulting congestion from idling engines adds to the particulate matter, which citizens are increasingly inhaling in dangerous quantities. This first national household survey has offered practical, if obvious, tips. Its value would be enhanced if planners converted these findings into actionable policy.   Topics : Public Transport NSO Business Standard Editorial Comment BS Opinion Transportation Buses

entry.title: Shifting immigration rules
entry.content:
Home / Opinion / Editorial / Shifting immigration rulesShifting immigration rules

Indian IT firms are prepared for the change

premium

The US suspension of eight tech companies, including Infosys, TCS, Wipro and HCLTech, from the PERM programme is expected to have limited immediate impact on Indian IT firms, which have reduced their dependence on H1B visas | Image Credit: Bloomberg

Business Standard Editorial Comment3 min read Last Updated : Oct 14 2026 | 10:18 PM ISTThe recent decision by the United States (US) to suspend eight tech companies, including Infosys, Tata Consultancy Services (TCS), Wipro and HCL Tech, from the Permanent Labour Certification (Perm) programme strikes a discordant note in relation to the treatment of highly skilled foreign professionals. As the Ministry of External Affairs has said, the restrictive move hinders the shared ambition between the two countries. Since 2005, when Perm came into effect, it has helped reduce the processing time for an employer in the US to sponsor a foreign worker for permanent residency or the green card. The adverse impact of the suspension of the programme on Indian information-technology (IT) firms and their employees cannot be overlooked, though many top companies have said that the repercussions of the US action on them will not be significant.  Although the move is being interpreted as a worrying signal overall, Indian IT majors have been in a state of readiness for such an eventuality. This should minimise any harm arising from the Perm suspension. The action could also accelerate the prospects of research & development as well as engineering jobs shifting to the global capability centres (GCCs) in India. In a statement, Nasscom, the leading association of the Indian tech industry, asserted that companies had reduced their dependence on the H1B visa in recent years while stepping up their hiring in the US. It has underscored the fact that the number of workers moving from the H1B visa to permanent residency through Perm is not high. TCS, India’s largest IT-services exporter, expressed similar sentiments, stating that the action by the US administration wouldn’t disturb its workforce strategy. Infosys, Wipro and HCL too have been on the same page, claiming that the suspension would have no material impact on the companies’ operations.  Estimates suggest Indian IT firms constituted less than 2 per cent of the Perm applications filed between October 2024 and September 2025. This implies that they may not be impacted in the near term, but the fallout could be felt in the longer run in terms of higher hiring cost and rising compliance-related expenses because they would need to depend majorly on local talent in the US. Anticipating changes in the US administration, large Indian tech companies have been changing their work models. The numbers for H1B visa registration reflect the change. The top six Indian IT firms, for instance, recorded a 92 per cent decline in numbers during FY27 over the previous year. From 21,919, the registrations dropped to 1,763.  The US has been tightening the immigration system with measures such as a $100,000 fee for certain visas, changes in the H1B lottery system, and a rule to end the automatic renewal of work permits for some immigrants, prompting Indian tech companies to prepare for a future that’s very different from the body-shop model they followed till recently. But with the latest action, the tech-job market may see a churn as a pathway to the green card disappears from the horizon. Beyond the business and economic implications, the green-card restrictions came with offensive remarks by US Vice-President J D Vance and Labour Secretary Keith Sonderling. While Mr Vance called tech workers “foreign indentured servants”, Mr Sonderling said jobs in the US would not go to “foreign fraudsters’’. With foreigners, including several Indian-origin professionals, running top firms in the US, those statements expose the nature and thinking of the US administration.   Topics : BS Opinion Business Standard Editorial Comment Trump’s immigration agenda US immigration IT companies

Today's columns examine India's failure to use its skilled diaspora, succession challenges in family businesses, Rahul Gandhi's political strategy, and resistance to resource-intensive data centres

Illustration: Binay Sinha

Tanmaya Nanda New Delhi 3 min read Last Updated : Oct 17 2026 | 6:15 AM ISTHello and welcome to Best of Business Standard Opinion, our wrap of the day's editorial page.  Shyam Saran contrasts China’s success in building scientific and technological capabilities with India’s failure to harness its skilled diaspora. Deng Xiaoping’s reforms combined investment in education and research with technology transfers, overseas study and collaboration between foreign experts and Chinese institutions. India, by contrast, often fails to provide returning professionals with adequate research facilities or a welcoming institutional environment. Saran argues that promoting skilled migration while struggling to create meaningful domestic employment reflects a policy failure. With artificial intelligence becoming strategically crucial, he urges India to expand its existing centres of excellence and attract overseas talent to strengthen its scientific and technological capabilities.  Family-owned businesses face a persistent tension between cultural preferences for family leadership and the need to appoint the most competent executives. Succession requires clear distinctions between ownership, governance and management, alongside rigorous assessment and mentoring of potential heirs. R Gopalakrishnan recommends succession committees comprising family members and independent directors, with successors tested through challenging assignments and professional chief executives appropriately recognised. Brazil’s JBS offers an example: after its founder’s sons presided over rapid expansion and a corruption scandal, professional CEO Gilberto Tomazoni led the company for eight years before handing over to the founder’s grandson, who had undergone extensive grooming. Rahul Gandhi’s political prospects present a paradox: while BJP supporters dismiss him, Narendra Modi and Amit Shah treat the Congress leader as a serious challenger. The Congress retains a substantial vote base, and Shekhar Gupta argues that even a modest increase could significantly alter parliamentary arithmetic. But street mobilisation and allegations of electoral manipulation cannot substitute for a constructive alternative. With 2029 approaching, Gupta challenges Rahul to spell out policies on institutions, foreign affairs, jobs, caste, education, economic reform and minority inclusion. He might consider adopting a UK-style shadow cabinet to develop credible alternatives, given that criticism of Modi alone will not suffice. Growing resistance to data centres reflects their heavy consumption of power and water, limited job creation and concerns over privacy and political favouritism. Ukrainian drone attacks on Yandex facilities in Russia also highlight their vulnerability and potential role in hosting malicious online activity. In the US, opposition has become bipartisan, with some states considering moratoriums, while European projects face delays. Devangshu Datta cautions that India, despite the opportunity to attract investments displaced from Western markets, faces tighter resource constraints. Local resistance could grow if communities see few benefits, and might even limit losses if the AI investment boom collapses.

entry.title: Of bots, watts, and water
entry.content:
Home / Opinion / Columns / Of bots, watts, and waterOf bots, watts, and water

Growing opposition to data centres in the US and Europe could create opportunities for India, but high power and water consumption, limited job creation and local resistance pose significant risks.

premium

Growing opposition to data centres in the US and Europe could benefit India's expanding AI infrastructure sector, although concerns over power consumption, water resources and limited job creation remain | Representative Image

Devangshu Datta4 min read Last Updated : Oct 16 2026 | 11:10 PM ISTBetween October 7 and 11, Ukraine launched successful drone attacks on three major data centres in Russia. All three centres were run by “Russia’s Google”, Yandex. The attacks caused significant physical damage, resulting in global traffic attributable to Yandex falling by 99 per cent on October 12 before recovering to 85 per cent of normal levels by October 14.  According to some data analysts, one outcome of Yandex going down was a decline in right-wing troll and bot traffic across social media. Organisations like Germany’s AFD Party and the United States’ Republican Party are said to have suffered loss of engagement for a few days. However, other analysts say malicious bot traffic just relocated to other Cloud service providers.  Yandex, as mentioned above, is referred to as Russia’s Google even though it had just $20 billion in revenue in 2025, which is minuscule compared to Alphabet’s $402 billion. But Yandex does offer a similar portfolio of services. It runs a (regime-friendly) search engine, hosts websites (and bots) on its Cloud, and offers email services, among other things. It also offers the services of Yandex AI, which is described as “an all-in-one mobile assistant, search engine, and chatbot app… which combines real-time web search with generative AI capabilities into a single interface.”  Data centres are required for all this. They run AI, back up, process and analyse data, and host Cloud services. They also consume vast quantities of power and water. They employ very few people. A multi-billion-dollar data centre may employ less than a dozen.  Quite aside from performing dodgy functions like hosting bots and troll factories, data centres have become a contentious issue in America’s midterm elections due to their infrastructure footprint. Ginormous power and water consumption translates into pressure on local infrastructure and potentially, higher tariffs. Lack of local employment generation equates to a lack of rationale for tolerating local data centres. There’s also been enough publicity about AI eating jobs to generate fears of net job losses as data centres proliferate.  Opinion polls suggest this dislike is bipartisan: US voters dislike data centres regardless of political affiliations. It’s turned into what’s called a NIMBY (not in my back yard) issue. By some accounts and according to some polls, more Americans would be comfortable with a nuclear power plant than with a data centre in their zip code. (Incidentally, the power demands of data centres could result in more investments in nuclear plants.)  New York has a moratorium on data centres and another 14 US states (some red, some blue) are considering bans or moratoriums. Recent reportage suggests that in addition to the fears of elevated tariffs and negative employment impact, US citizens are less than happy about potential loss of privacy. Many also suspect that local politicians were “on the take” because many data centres got favourable terms and some were set up under non-disclosure agreements.  Will the American dislike for data centres lead to a halt in AI deployment? No, of course not! Data centre projects are being located all over the world and the pace of data centre capex is supposed to accelerate, on paper, at least. But there’s resistance in other locations as well. Some 70-odd projects are now delayed across Europe due to local NIMBY resistance.  This antipathy will probably be presented as a great opportunity for digital India. There are already several Indian mega data-centre projects in various stages of planning and execution and more projects could relocate out of the First World.  What could go wrong? Well, India is far more stretched than the US or the European Union when it comes to power and water resources. Indians will not be suspicious about politicians collecting kickbacks for large projects; they will take it for granted.  Corruption is tolerated where there’s some apparent benefit, such as in the tender for a new road where easier commuting is a payoff. But a data centre doesn’t create many benefits and may indeed lead to net employment losses and deterioration in local power and water resources. So, corruption could become a sore point.  Is it far-fetched to imagine a backlash? Indians have objected to port projects, copper smelters, nuclear plants. They might object to data centres.  Looking at it cynically, protests that slow down projects may actually do India a favour under some circumstances. If the AI bubble does burst, investments into data centres will have to be written off. A project that aborts early, for whatever reason, will lose less money. 
 The writer is a New Delhi-based independent journalist.   Disclaimer: These are personal views of the writer. They do not necessarily reflect the opinion of www.business-standard.com or the Business Standard newspaperTopics : Data centre Russia Ukraine Conflict BS Opinion artifical intelligence

entry.title: India says cheese
entry.content:
Home / Opinion / Columns / India says cheeseIndia says cheese

These makers are translating, not copying, the western varieties. One Chennai cheesemaker coats cheddar with milagai podi, a South Indian chilli-and-lentil powder

premium

Photo: Shutterstock

Kumar Abishek5 min read Last Updated : Oct 16 2026 | 10:26 PM ISTThere are gifts for the president of Switzerland other than cheese. Still, when Prime Minister Narendra Modi gave Guy Parmelin three award-winning cheeses in New Delhi on October 5, the gift sent a quiet message. Gulmarg, Konark and Yeoor, made by Mumbai’s Eleftheria Cheese, had won medals overseas, two in Bern, the capital of Gruyère and Emmental country. India appeared to have something to share on the cheeseboard.  Gulmarg is a Brie-style, heart-shaped cheese with a snowy, velvety rind, aged for two-three weeks. Konark is a tomme shaped like the chariot wheel of Odisha’s Sun Temple; and Yeoor, a rose-rind mountain cheese aged for eight-nine months in the Gruyère tradition. For a country that’s famous overseas for paneer in curries and sliced cheese on burgers, the gift was a small revelation. India’s cheese story, however, began long before its new cheesemakers.  Dairy traces in Harappan pottery from Kotada Bhadli, Gujarat, show that people processed milk about 4,500 years ago. The findings, however, have limits: They show people could handle milk, but that does not mean Harappans made cheese like cheddar. Vedic writings talk about āmikṣā, a mass made by curdling milk with sour milk, and vājina, the whey that remains. The basic principle of cheesemaking was already there, but India took a different path.  Practical reasons mattered — aged cheese needs cellars, but much of the subcontinent is hot and humid. Traditional rennet made from calf stomachs also did not fit well in a culture that reveres cows and has a large vegetarian population. Also, ghee and curd handled preservation and nutrition exceptionally well. Furthermore, in Vedic traditions and broader Indian culture, splitting milk was seen as inauspicious, yet a repertoire of fresh and dried cheeses grew to fill the aged varieties’ void.  In Jammu, Gujjar shepherds make kalari by curdling milk with whey and drying the rounds so they can be fried in their own fat. In the Himalayas, chhurpi is cooked, pressed, and dried until it is hard as rock so it can last years. In Gujarat, Parsi families drain topli paneer in wicker baskets. The steps are familiar to cheesemakers everywhere: Warm, curdle, drain, shape and preserve. But the sun and smoke replace the need for a cellar.  Persian and Central Asian influences are often credited with popularising paneer, but the evidence is weak. In Bengal, the popular story credits the Portuguese with introducing acid-curdling, giving rise to chhena and, eventually, rasgulla and sandesh. But historians disagree; Bandel, a salty, smoked cheese named after the old Portuguese settlement near Hooghly, is a more tangible legacy. Around Kalimpong, Swiss missionaries left a modest Gouda-like tradition. India had plenty of cheese, but its many styles never came together in one national market.  Then came the White Revolution: Operation Flood in the 1970s — led by Verghese Kurien and dairy cooperatives — turned India into a milk leader. Amul first brought cheese to the masses. Britannia and Mother Dairy followed. For years, cheese came in a tin, a packet, or as a slice, made to melt and last long. Pizza shops brought mozzarella to homes in the mid-1990s, but handmade, aged cheese stayed a niche pursuit.  Making cheese is exacting: Starter cultures turn milk sugar into lactic acid; rennet sets the milk; and cut curds release whey before stirring, heating, draining and salting determine the texture. Some cheeses are eaten fresh; others age for months, with temperature and humidity shaping their rind and taste. In India’s heat, a good cold chain is needed to transform an experiment to a viable product.  The serious artisanal shift started 15 years ago, in small kitchens and creameries. Some people who returned from abroad missed the cheeses they had tasted, and social entrepreneurs saw a chance to make money from pastoral milk. A Kashmir business that began with western styles went on to champion kalari. In Rajasthan, an enterprise working with the Raika community turns camel milk into feta and cream cheese. A Chennai creamery buys milk from herders and helps build the supply chain.  These makers are translating, not copying, the western varieties. One Chennai cheesemaker coats cheddar with milagai podi, a South Indian chilli-and-lentil powder, and recommends grating it over a dosa. A Uttarakhand farm mixes spices into its cheese. A Bengaluru brewpub swaps cream for burrata in butter chicken. With flavours in the mix, borrowed names matter less; Indian milk and tastes can stand on their own.  International judges have taken note, too. Eleftheria’s Norwegian-style brown whey cheese won India’s first World Cheese Awards silver in 2021. Its cloth-bound cheddar, Moony, won gold in 2022. Konark won gold in 2023, and silver in Bern in 2025 (alongside Yeoor), while Gulmarg won Super Gold in Brazil this year. Desi Dairy Dialogue now brings makers, herders and cheesemongers together.  Calling artisanal cheesemaking a revolution would overstate the numbers, as per capita consumption remains low and processed cheese dominates supermarket shelves. The change is quieter: Sun-dried and smoked cheeses now sit alongside factory slices and cellar-aged wheels. A country that began separating curds from whey 4,500 years ago is learning to give cheese time. The three Indian cheeses on the Swiss president’s table suggest how far that journey has come.

Today's editorials and columns examine the IDBI Bank privatisation deal, India's steel ambitions, tribunal reforms, AI-driven infrastructure improvements and a book on the changing geopolitical order

Illustration: Binay SInha

Tanmaya Nanda New Delhi 3 min read Last Updated : Oct 16 2026 | 6:15 AM ISTHello and welcome to Best of Business Standard Opinion, our wrap of the day's editorial page. The Cabinet Committee on Economic Affairs has approved the strategic sale of IDBI Bank, with Toronto-based Fairfax Financial Holdings set to acquire a 60.72 per cent stake for ₹52,878 crore. The deal, the largest foreign direct investment in India’s financial sector to date, offers an opportunity to revive the government’s stalled privatisation programme. Only 21 strategic sales have occurred in 26 years, while the number of central public-sector enterprises has risen. Today's first editorial argues that privatisation would free public resources and reduce fiscal burdens. It urges the government to sell its residual IDBI stake and accelerate equity sales in other public-sector companies. The draft National Steel Policy: Vision 2047 targets crude steel capacity of 604 million tonnes by 2047, but today's second editorial cautions that expansion must be matched by raw-material security, cleaner technology and global competitiveness. With India importing 92 per cent of its coking coal, greater reliance on conventional steelmaking could deepen import dependence and emissions. The policy’s proposals on scrap, renewable energy and hydrogen-based production need commercially viable implementation. Protection against unfair imports must not weaken incentives to improve productivity, particularly as carbon-related trade barriers spread. Our editorial also questions production-linked incentives, stressing that success depends on efficiency, innovation and higher-value products. India’s tribunals suffer from inadequate infrastructure, vacancies and administrative shortcomings, undermining their ability to deliver timely, specialised justice. K P Krishnan argues that the proposed National Tribunals Commission (NTC) must address these systemic failures rather than function merely as a personnel and oversight body. Drawing on the UK’s Courts and Tribunals Service and India’s Passport Seva model, he advocates separating judicial decision-making from administrative support. A professionally managed institution should handle procurement, infrastructure, technology and staffing, allowing judges to focus on adjudication. The NTC legislation offers an opportunity to build this institutional capacity and strengthen state capability across the economy. India’s artificial intelligence (AI) dividend could lie as much in improving existing infrastructure as in building new technology. Vinayak Chatterjee explores how machine learning, predictive maintenance and computer vision can help power networks, water systems, roads and railways detect faults early, reduce losses and improve reliability. India’s smart-meter rollout and Jal Jeevan Mission offer opportunities to apply these tools at scale, while examples from Sweden, Britain and Italy demonstrate their potential. However, fragmented records, incompatible systems and cybersecurity risks remain obstacles. Chatterjee advocates starting with targeted pilots, measuring operational gains and retaining human oversight, arguing that reliable data and effective implementation matter more than technological novelty. In The World in Turmoil: Why Geopolitics Matters, John Andrews examines how geography, resources, demography and climate shape international relations. Chintan Girish Modi finds the book a useful guide to concepts ranging from hard and soft power to debt diplomacy, nuclear deterrence and multipolarity, making it valuable for students, journalists and general readers. Andrews’s provocative questioning of the Global South’s coherence offers India food for thought as it seeks a larger global role. However, the review notes the book’s limited engagement with feminist perspectives and the UN’s Women, Peace and Security framework, while criticising its use of masculinist language to describe military destruction.

entry.title: Getting AI into infrastructure
entry.content:
Home / Opinion / Columns / Getting AI into infrastructureGetting AI into infrastructure

It can improve the reliability, efficiency and performance of the systems we already have

premium

AI technology can help improve infrastructure efficiency through smarter monitoring, early fault detection and predictive maintenance

Vinayak Chatterjee5 min read Last Updated : Oct 15 2026 | 10:23 PM ISTIndia’s artificial intelligence (AI) conversation is dominated by startups, foundation models, semiconductors, data centres, chips, chatbots and humanoid robots. These investments matter. But a major AI dividend may come from a less glamorous source: The brownfield infrastructure assets already in service.  Power networks, water systems, roads and railways hold years of operating history, yet information about them is often scattered across sensors, software, spreadsheets and paper. Applying AI to these assets is harder than deploying it in a new project: Equipment cannot simply be switched off, and poor recommendations can affect safety and reliability.  But better forecasts, earlier fault detection and more informed maintenance can make existing systems work better. AI in infrastructure is not one technology: Machine-learning models can forecast demand or equipment failure, computer vision can inspect assets, and analytical tools can help operators interpret data.  AI can also aid project planning by estimating schedules, resource needs and cost overruns. At construction sites, computer vision can flag hazards and check progress and quality; drones can inspect hard-to-reach areas. In operating systems, predictive maintenance can help teams act before equipment fails. Weather models can improve wind and solar forecasts, while traffic analytics can support more responsive urban transport.  India’s power-distribution network shows the potential. Under the Revamped Distribution Sector Scheme, India is installing nearly 200 million prepaid smart meters, more than 5.2 million distribution-transformer meters and around 210,000 feeder meters. Together, these devices can provide a continuous view of network conditions.  Combining meter, feeder, weather and asset data can reveal unusual consumption, overloaded feeders, technical losses or early signs of equipment failure. Analytics could flag a vulnerable transformer, recommend load rebalancing and help position a field crew before a fault becomes an outage. Ideally, customers would never notice the interruption that was prevented.  Water is another promising application. The Jal Jeevan Mission aims to connect 190 million rural households to piped drinking water. Sensors can help monitor the quantity, quality and regularity of supply. AI could identify leaks, detect unusual pump behaviour and show where service is falling short from the source through the network to household taps.  International examples offer practical lessons. In Sweden, water utility VA SYD trained AI to monitor 2,000 kilometres of pipes. Siemens reports that water loss fell from 10 per cent to 8 per cent, while smaller leaks could be detected before bursts.  In Britain, Network Rail is developing its INSIGHT decision-support tool to help frontline teams diagnose track problems earlier; the organisation says it could save more than £30 million a year. Italy’s Enel uses AI and computer vision to identify grid components and anomalies, helping teams distinguish routine inspections from urgent maintenance.  The International Energy Agency estimates that AI-based fault detection could reduce outage durations by 30-50 per cent, while digital tools could unlock up to 175 Gw of transmission capacity without building new lines. These are estimates of potential, not guaranteed outcomes; results depend on the assets, data and operational response.  The challenge is that brownfield information is rarely ready for AI. Asset records may be incomplete, identifiers inconsistent and data trapped in disconnected systems. Infrastructure must keep running while improvements are made. Operators, therefore, need dependable, secure and usable data, not simply a large “data lake.”  Clear asset registers, reliable records, interoperable systems and accountable data ownership are more useful starting points. Organisations should select the method that fits the task: A forecasting or anomaly-detection model may solve an equipment problem more simply than a large language model. Language models can help staff search manuals or maintenance histories, but they cannot substitute for accurate operational data or engineering judgement.  Cybersecurity must be designed in from the start. Connecting systems can widen the attack surface, particularly where (IT meets operational technology. Strong access controls, network separation, monitoring and recovery plans are essential. So is frontline involvement: Engineers and field workers can identify operating conditions that may be invisible in the data.  A sensible path is to start with one high-value use case, establish a baseline and run a controlled pilot. Measure results that matter — outage time, water loss, equipment failures, inspection effort, false alarms and repair costs. Keep people responsible for consequential decisions, define a safe fallback and expand only when the pilot demonstrates reliable value.  Procurement should also specify who owns the data, how systems interoperate, and how performance can be audited. Models must be tested regularly as assets, operating patterns and weather conditions change. An alert has value only when a named team can verify it and act within a timeframe.  The countries that benefit most from AI will connect intelligence to productive assets at scale. India should continue building new infrastructure while making existing systems more reliable, efficient and responsive. The AI dividend will not be won only in data centres. It will also be won in the control room that catches a fault early, beneath the road where a leak is found before a burst, and at the bus stop where services arrive when expected.

The window to legislate on tribunals is a golden opportunity to rethink their administration and that of the judiciary as a whole

premium

Illustration: Binay SInha

K P Krishnan6 min read Last Updated : Oct 15 2026 | 10:11 PM ISTEveryone wants more state capability. A vital area for injecting improvements into state capability is the judiciary. When we make the judiciary better, we trigger improvements everywhere.  An important battle in legal system reforms concerns the tribunals. While hearing a recent matter regarding the National Company Law Tribunal (NCLT), newspapers reported that the Supreme Court (SC) of India posed a pointed question to the government: “How will tribunals function if there is no infrastructure? Every day they deal with thousands of crores of issues... They are the government’s lifeline.” Even more worrisome is the announcement by the NCLT Mumbai Bench regarding the suspension of Court VI effective October 13 due to a shortage of tribunal members!  We in India are too quick to create government organisations, including regulators and tribunals. But all too often, the follow through, by way of organisational design and thorough implementation, has been lacking.  Tribunals were originally conceived as an institutional innovation to solve two distinct problems in the Indian legal system. First, the traditional courts, particularly the high courts, were buckling under an unsustainable caseload. Second, when faced with the increasing complexity of a modernising, liberalised economy, it was felt that specialised knowledge of judges in tribunals would help.  Whether determining fair tariffs in the electricity sector, adjudicating anti-competitive behaviour in digital markets, or resolving complex corporate insolvencies, modern disputes demand a nuanced understanding of economics, accounting, and domain-specific mechanics. By designing tribunals that paired judicial members with technical experts, policy designers hoped to deliver faster, expert-driven adjudication.  The Supreme Court generally viewed this parallel judicial apparatus with apprehension. The transfer of adjudicatory powers from traditional constitutional courts to executive-appointed tribunals raises legitimate questions regarding the separation of powers and judicial independence. The higher judiciary expressed these concerns but responded pragmatically with a certain “wait and see” approach.  The bargain implicitly struck between the judiciary and the executive has frayed over time. The behaviour of the executive on operational issues —ranging from the timely appointment of members to the provision of resources for a functioning office — has frustrated the possibility of properly functioning tribunals. The chronic failures of many tribunals drove the SC to force the creation of an independent National Tribunals Commission (NTC) to oversee the administration of these bodies.  The most compelling international template for this endeavour is the United Kingdom’s Her Majesty’s Courts and Tribunals Service (HMCTS). The HMCTS is a dedicated agency jointly owned and operated by the higher judiciary and the executive government. Its mandate is unambiguous: To ensure that all administrative, logistical, and infrastructural requirements of the courts and tribunals are met seamlessly. Whether it involves setting up a newly created tribunal, expanding existing Benches to manage a surging workload, or deploying modern digital case management systems, the HMCTS serves as the institutional engine.  What makes the HMCTS highly effective is its managerial and commercial capabilities. It is manned not by judicial officers, but by seasoned management professionals. These professionals possess procurement capabilities of a high order, enabling them to execute a transparent, cost-effective acquisition of goods and services, which is the most important requirement of such public agencies. They handle real estate, IT infrastructure, human resources for registry staff, and all such day-to-day operations. Similar mechanisms, with a separation between the judicial and administrative functions of a court, are used by most developed countries.  By isolating administration from adjudication, this model optimises the deployment of a scarce and highly valuable resource: Judicial talent. A core flaw in the Indian system has been the burdening of senior judges with administrative trivia. Judicial officers are not, and should not be expected to be, experts in tender processes, civil construction, or vendor management. Expecting a tribunal chair to manage infrastructure procurement is like asking an expert neurosurgeon to perform complex brain surgery while simultaneously holding her responsible for procuring the hospital’s detergents and managing the nursing roster. It is a gross misallocation of specialised and scarce human capital.  If looking to the UK seems too distant, we need only look closer to home to find a spectacularly successful model of bifurcating specialised (sovereign) functions from logistical support: The Passport Seva system, executed via a public-private partnership between the Ministry of External Affairs (MEA) and a private company.  Before this reform, passport issuance was a notorious bureaucratic bottleneck. The MEA recognised that the process involved two distinct types of work. The first was the administrative heavy-lifting: Managing appointments, physical infrastructure, queuing, biometric data collection, and document digitisation. The second was the core sovereign function: The legal and security determination of whether an individual should be granted an Indian passport. By bringing in a private company to carry out all the non-sovereign, logistical, and support functions, the MEA revolutionised the citizen experience. The private partner manages the facilities and the technology, operating with private-sector efficiency. Meanwhile, the critical, sovereign decision to issue or renew a passport remains entirely in the hands of the government officer.  We are now at a remarkable moment in Indian history where Parliament is taking legislative steps to implement the NTC. We must approach this possibility on a bigger scale than is envisaged in the present Bill, which envisions the NTC essentially as a personnel and oversight body. Administration and infrastructure in the comprehensive sense discussed above — which is the core bottleneck — is not proposed to be given to the NTC according to the Bill. This subject continues to be housed in the parent ministries.  The proposed NTC must be designed around the identical philosophical pivot of the passport project. The NTC should operate as the MEA equivalent of the tribunal system and discharge the core sovereign functions. The Bill should create an Indian equivalent of the HMCTS to manage the non-sovereign support functions, ensuring high-quality infrastructure and dynamically expanding capacity where case pendency demands it. Given India’s Constitutional scheme and the role of the state governments, we may need more than one entity.  This is one of the most consequential frontiers of state-building in India.

Today's editorials and columns examine US restrictions on Indian IT firms, India's public transport gaps, the Tata Sons leadership dispute, municipal governance under PRAGATI-50 and a book on Bastar

Bombay House, the headquarters of the Tata group

Tanmaya Nanda New Delhi 3 min read Last Updated : Oct 15 2026 | 6:15 AM ISTHello and welcome to Best of Business Standard Opinion, our wrap of the day's editorial page.  The United States' suspension of eight technology companies, including Infosys, Tata Consultancy Services, Wipro and HCL Tech, from the Permanent Labour Certification (PERM) programme threatens a pathway to green cards for skilled foreign workers. While Indian IT majors expect limited immediate impact, the move could raise hiring and compliance costs over time. Nasscom notes that firms have reduced H-1B dependence and increased local US hiring, with registrations by six leading Indian IT firms falling 92 per cent in financial year 2027. Today's first editorial warns that the restrictions, compounded by disparaging remarks from US officials, undermine the shared ambitions of the two countries.  The first all-India household travel survey by the National Statistics Office exposes India’s inadequate public transport and inequitable urban development. Only 15 per cent of workers use public transport, while 46 per cent rely on two-wheelers or cars. Commuting costs average Rs 785 monthly, rising to Rs 1,044 for urban workers, squeezing household incomes. The second editorial argues that poor transport networks and unaffordable housing force workers into unhealthy settlements far from employment centres. Greater investment in safe, extensive public transport and low-cost housing could widen employment opportunities, particularly for women. Better public transport would also ease congestion and pollution. The survey’s findings must translate into actionable policy. The leadership dispute at Tata Sons reflects a breakdown in governance, with differences among Tata Trusts trustees spilling into the holding company’s board. Laveesh Bhandari examines how the group’s tradition of absorbing professional managers into its wider family ecosystem can blur accountability and weaken the chain of command. With Air India still loss-making, Tata Digital seeking direction, Tata Electronics making major bets and artificial intelligence challenging TCS, the group needs decisive leadership. Bhandari rejects a split or compromise arrangement, arguing that the professional heading Tata Sons must have strategic autonomy, clear accountability and the confidence of Tata Trusts, while remaining at arm’s length from its ownership. PRAGATI-50, launched on September 29, seeks to sustain visible cleanliness across 50 cities, building on Swachh Bharat Mission’s gains in waste processing and collection. Amit Kapoor argues that lasting progress depends less on campaigns and targets than on municipal capacity. Audits reveal staff shortages, limited recruitment powers, weak revenues and fragmented control over urban services. New waste-management rules also risk burdening households without ensuring cities have adequate infrastructure, while waste pickers could be displaced by mechanisation. Kapoor calls for stronger municipal finances, clearer accountability, professional staffing and regional facilities, with monitoring that measures institutional capacity alongside visible outcomes. Larger cities should mentor smaller towns. Shantanu Nandan Sharma’s Rebel Bastar: History, Maoism and the search for answers in India’s Heartland draws on extensive field reporting, archival records and colonial accounts to illuminate the history, politics and tribal culture of a region that remains poorly understood. Aditi Phadnis praises its account of Bastar’s dynasties, British exploitation, the Bhumkal uprising and the enduring legacy of tribal hero Gunda Dhur. The book’s strongest section explores how Maoism took root among Bastar’s communities, shaped by their distinctive beliefs and social fabric, which the author calls the Mahua ideology. Phadnis finds the lengthy detour into Mao’s history unnecessary but considers the book outstanding for its research, despite structural weaknesses.
